note.question: How should a donor allocate a limited antimalarial subsidy budget when a retailer can deceptively mix lower-cost uncertified drugs with certified treatments?
note.overview: A donor commits to purchase and sales subsidies under a budget, anticipating a retailer’s strategic sourcing, inventory, and pricing response between certified and uncertified drugs. The paper treats this as a sequential game-theoretic supply-chain model; upstream suppliers and consumers are not strategic players.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: At the outset the donor chooses per-unit purchase subsidy a and sales subsidy s under a budget. In each period the retailer observes inventory, orders a mix before demand uncertainty resolves, observes the market condition, sets price when permitted, sells randomly from the pooled stock, and carries leftovers forward. Purchase subsidies lower only certified acquisition cost, whereas sales subsidies can reward sales from either source. Deception makes consumer demand depend on pooled expected quality rather than realized drug type.

models.relation: This is an alternative to A donor-retailer leader-follower game with dynamic sourcing, pricing, and inventory under counterfeit risk.
models.summary: Second, we note the potential for consumers to be worse off when donors focus on the objective of eliminating uncertified drugs. In other words, a higher penalty cost is incurred for sourcing a greater fraction of counterfeit drugs or for sourcing counterfeit drugs of lower quality. Specifically, even when restricted to certified drugs, higher sales subsidies still increase the average profit margin per unit sold.23 These dynamics thereby continue to influence the retailer’s decisions depending on stock-out sensitivity and discount factor, similar to cases in which sales subsidies apply to all drugs.

conditions: When B ≥ ̃B l 1, a purchase subsidy alone is sufficient to incentivize the retailer to switch from sourcing uncertified drugs to certified drugs.
With limited budgets and high-quality uncertified drugs available (e.g., α ≪θ ≈1), sales subsidies become optimal as they indirectly support these drugs’ distribution.

In fact, when budget limitations cannot be addressed and falsified counterfeit drugs are prevalent, donors should concentrate their spending in fewer locations (rather than spreading their budget thinly) and offer purchase subsidies in order to incentivize retailers to purchase certified drugs.
